subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x(x + 3)e^(−x/2) on [−3, 0].

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what you take out as a common factor after differentiating, and which root you reject.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Check the conditions on [−3, 0]
steps.margin_note: First mark. Anything multiplied by 0 is 0, whatever the exponential is worth. Write the zero bracket instead of working out a decimal for e^(3/2).
steps.memory_tip: e raised to any real power is positive, never zero, so a product with an exponential is zero only where the other factor is zero.
lines: (i) x² + 3x is a polynomial and e^(−x/2) is an exponential function; both are continuous for every real x, so f is continuous on [−3, 0]
(ii) both are differentiable for every real x, so f is differentiable on (−3, 0)
∴ f(−3) = f(0) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies on [−3, 0].

recall.must_convey: That the polynomial and the exponential are both continuous and differentiable everywhere, and that f(−3) = f(0) = 0 because the polynomial factor is zero at each end.
accept: both factors are continuous and differentiable for every real x
at minus three the bracket x plus three is zero so f is zero
at zero the factor x is zero so f is zero
rendu ends lo polynomial factor zero kabatti f zero avuthundi
the exponential is never zero so only the polynomial matters at the ends

steps.why: The exponential factor is never zero, so the end values come entirely from the polynomial part — and −3 and 0 are exactly its two roots. Saying so is quicker and safer than evaluating e^(3/2) as a decimal.
common_mistakes: Working out e^(3/2) as a decimal when the other factor is already 0.

steps.label: Differentiate and test the roots
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Rejecting x = 3 is part of the answer, not a detail — c has to lie strictly inside (−3, 0). Say which root is rejected and why.
steps.memory_tip: Take the exponential out as a common factor first; only the bracket that is left can be zero.
lines: e^(−x/2) > 0 for every real x, so f′(x) = 0 ⇒ (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or x = −2
x = 3 does not lie in (−3, 0), so it is rejected; x = −2 lies in (−3, 0)

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified, with c = −2 ∈ (−3, 0)

recall.must_convey: That the product rule gives f′(x) = −(e^(−x/2)/2)(x − 3)(x + 2), that the exponential is never zero, and that x = 3 is rejected leaving c = −2.
accept: use the product rule and take the exponential out as a common factor
the exponential is never zero so only the quadratic bracket can vanish
the roots are three and minus two, and three is outside so reject it
three interval bayata undi kabatti reject cheyyali, c minus two
c equals minus two which is inside minus three to zero

steps.why: The product rule leaves e^(−x/2) in both terms, and taking it out is what turns the equation into a quadratic. Since an exponential is never zero, every root of f′ has to come from the bracket that remains.
common_mistakes: Differentiating e^(−x/2) as e^(−x/2) and losing the factor −1/2 from the chain rule.
Setting e^(−x/2) = 0 and trying to solve it, when an exponential is never zero.
Keeping x = 3 as an answer; it is outside [−3, 0] and must be rejected.
